title: Rising real estate prices warrant monitoring: CBSL | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 5 November 2026 06:43
-     - 23

The continued upward trend in real estate prices, together with the banking sector’s increasing exposure to real estate activities, warrants continued monitoring, the Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) said, warning that a sharp correction in property prices could spill over to the financial system.

In its recent Financial Stability Review 2026, the CBSL said Asking Price Indices for land, houses and condominiums in the Colombo District, which track the prices sought by sellers against a 2019 base, continued to increase during most of the review period, with all three reaching their highest levels since 2019.

The upward movement reflected improving economic activity, elevated construction costs and sustained demand for real estate assets, supported by lower borrowing costs amid relatively accommodative monetary policy conditions, the CBSL said. However, the persistent increase in property valuations highlighted the need for continued attention given the risk of potential market imbalances.

That backdrop has since shifted. The CBSL raised the Overnight Policy Rate (OPR) by 100 basis points to 8.75% on 26 May 2026, its first policy rate increase since June 2023, which the report said contributed to further upward adjustments in market interest rates and Government securities yields.

Meanwhile, the banking sector’s exposure to real estate related activities remained elevated, with loans extended to the sector accounting for 13.7% of total loans and advances by end-June 2026. Data in the report show total exposure approaching Rs. 2 trillion by end-June 2026, growing at a double-digit pace year-on-year. This marks a strong rebound from 2024, when exposure contracted, before returning to growth in 2025.

This exposure covers loans for the purchase of land, the construction, development and renovation of residential and non-residential buildings, and real estate activities including condominium development. Growth in real estate lending was primarily driven by residential real estate activities, which account for more than 80% of the exposure, while lending to non-residential real estate activities contracted.

Asset quality in the segment improved, however. The Stage 3 loans ratio of real estate lending, which captures credit-impaired loans, declined to 10.4% by end-June 2026 from 14% a year earlier, indicating an improvement in asset quality amid credit expansion. Even so, it remained above the banking sector’s overall Stage 3 loans ratio of 9.1%.

Construction more broadly remains a pressure point. The report noted that construction, which accounts for more than 10% of total banking sector credit, was among the sectors contributing over 10% of credit expansion during the year to end 2Q 2026, and continued to record a relatively high Stage 3 loans ratio, although it declined from a year earlier. Construction-related small and medium enterprises continued to register a Stage 3 loans ratio above 20%, reflecting persistent repayment challenges.

The CBSL listed the continued rise in real estate prices among emerging domestic risks, alongside rising household indebtedness and volatility in collateral values amid increased exposure to collateral-backed lending.

“Given the linkages between the real estate market and the banking sector, a sharp correction in property prices could adversely affect collateral values and borrower repayment capacity, creating negative spillover risks to financial stability,” the CBSL said.

title: Improving macroeconomy gives Group ‘more stable operating backdrop’: JKH Chairperson | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 5 November 2026 06:52
-     - 14

Krishan Balendra

Improving macroeconomic conditions have given John Keells Holdings PLC (JKH) a firmer footing for the quarters ahead, the conglomerate’s Chairperson Krishan Balendra told shareholders, pointing to stronger growth, rebuilt reserves and an upgraded sovereign credit rating as the base for the group’s operating environment.

In the statement accompanying the group’s interim results (https://www.ft.lk/top-story/JKH-2Q-PBT-up-2-to-Rs-7-95-b-attributable-profit-soars-213/26-799569), Balendra attributed the improvement squarely to reform. “Sri Lanka’s macroeconomic environment remained stable during the period under review, notwithstanding the volatile global external environment, reflecting the progress achieved from economic reforms and prudent policy management over the past several years,” he said.

“The economy continued its growth trajectory, with real GDP recording year-on-year growth of 4.2% in the second quarter of calendar year 2026, whilst gross official reserves remained resilient at approximately $ 6.9 billion as at end-September 2026.”

Fiscal performance also strengthened, with the Government recording surpluses on both the primary and budget balances as of August 2026, supported by revenue mobilisation, efforts to broaden the tax base and disciplined expenditure management.

Balendra flagged the upgrade of Sri Lanka’s sovereign credit rating by Fitch Ratings to ‘B-’ from ‘CCC+’ during the quarter as a turning point. “During the quarter, Sri Lanka’s sovereign credit rating was upgraded by Fitch Ratings to ‘B-’ from ‘CCC+’, a significant milestone that reflects the progress achieved in restoring macroeconomic stability,” he said.

The Seventh Review of the International Monetary Fund’s Extended Fund Facility concluded successfully with a staff-level agreement, with the next disbursement expected to be approved by the IMF Executive Board in November 2026.

Balendra drew a direct link between the macro recovery and business confidence. “Together with the continued strengthening of external sector fundamentals, these developments have enhanced confidence in the country’s economic outlook and provided a more stable foundation for growth.”

The Chairperson was careful to qualify the base case, warning that developments in the Middle East continued to weigh on the business environment, with higher global energy prices feeding inflation, compounded by the low base effect of last year’s deflationary conditions. “Higher fuel, energy and imported commodity prices consequently created input cost pressures across a broad range of industries and businesses,” he said.

The rupee, which came under pressure in the first quarter amid heightened external volatility, subsequently stabilised, while domestic interest rates remained broadly stable.

Consumer demand continued to improve, though Balendra said discretionary spending held back in parts of the market. “Consumer demand continued to improve, although discretionary spending remained measured across certain segments.”

He described the pass-through of stability to the wider economy as uneven. “Whilst macroeconomic conditions have improved considerably, the benefits of this stability, and resultant consumer confidence, are continuing to filter through the broader economy at varying rates.”

Tourism held up despite geopolitical uncertainty and disruption to regional air connectivity. Sri Lanka welcomed approximately 1.69 million visitors in the first nine months of 2026, a marginal decline of about 2% year-on-year, though arrivals as at 29 October were some 3% ahead of the corresponding period last year. Forward bookings across the group’s hotels in Sri Lanka and the Maldives for the winter season remain strong, provided connectivity through key regional transit hubs remains largely uninterrupted.

“Overall, the continued improving macroeconomic environment provides a more stable operating backdrop for the Group, notwithstanding continued external uncertainties and varying demand conditions across sectors,” Balendra said.

title: PUCSL proposes 1.46% electricity tariff hike for 4Q | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 5 November 2026 06:50
-     - 12

The Public Utilities Commission of Sri Lanka (PUCSL) has estimated a 1.46% increase in electricity tariffs for the fourth quarter of 2026 following its preliminary review of the National System Operator’s (NSO) bulk supply cost submission, down from an initial estimate of 2.88%.

The proposed adjustment is subject to further review, with the regulator inviting stakeholder comments on the cost submissions and the quarterly tariff revision ahead of a public consultation scheduled for today (5).

In its consultation document on the fourth-quarter tariff review, the PUCSL said the NSO’s latest bulk supply cost forecast, submitted on 7 October, amounted to Rs. 125.94 billion, down from Rs. 134.16 billion in its initial submission on 4 September.

The reduction was largely driven by a downward revision in forecast generation energy costs, which fell from Rs. 105.58 billion in the initial submission to Rs. 98.31 billion in the latest forecast. The NSO also revised its expected generation capacity costs down to Rs. 18.98 billion from Rs. 19.94 billion.

Based on the submissions received from the licensees, the regulator initially estimated a revenue shortfall of Rs. 4.44 billion for the quarter, translating into a required tariff increase of 2.88%.

However, following its preliminary assessment, the PUCSL identified several cost items requiring adjustment, reducing the estimated revenue shortfall to Rs. 2.25 billion and the required tariff increase to 1.46%.

Among the adjustments was a Rs. 669 million reduction in Electricity Generation Lanka’s (EGL) generation capacity cost, which the Commission identified as an increase arising outside the Power Purchase Agreement framework.

The regulator also excluded Rs. 1.07 billion in additional costs submitted by Electricity Distribution Lanka (EDL) relating to loan repayments for the Supporting Electricity Supply Reliability Improvement Project (SESRIP). The PUCSL said the cost was not allowable in principle as it related to capital work in progress, with such expenditure recoverable through tariffs only after the assets are completed and capitalised.

Another adjustment concerned the estimated additional cost arising from substandard coal used during the second quarter of 2026. While the NSO had estimated this at Rs. 2.86 billion, the PUCSL’s own estimate was higher at Rs. 4.38 billion.

After accounting for these adjustments, the Commission’s preliminary calculation puts total electricity supply costs for the fourth quarter at Rs. 156.66 billion, against estimated revenue of Rs. 154.03 billion at existing tariffs.

The regulator said the preliminary assessment would be subject to further examination, particularly regarding the adequacy of projected major hydro generation against rainfall forecasts, fuel prices used in cost estimates and the cost-effective utilisation of battery energy storage systems (BESS).

The NSO has forecast major hydro generation of 1,551 GWh during the quarter, accounting for 32.34% of total expected electricity generation. Renewable energy sources, excluding major hydro, are expected to contribute a further 28.81%, while coal is projected to account for 25.68%.

The forecast assumes above-normal rainfall in hydro catchment areas during October to December, based on the Department of Meteorology’s seasonal outlook. The Commission said the hydro generation assumptions would need to be verified against actual generation and water inflow data.

The regulator also noted that the NSO had factored in the connection of 160 MW of battery energy storage capacity during the final quarter, with Rs. 703 million allocated for capacity costs. However, the submission did not provide monthly electricity charging and discharging estimates.

On fuel costs, the consultation document highlighted a significant increase in coal prices compared with the previous tariff determination. Forecast coal prices rise from Rs. 61.42 per kg in October to Rs. 67.44 per kg in December, while diesel is estimated at Rs. 382 per litre and furnace oil at Rs. 210 per litre throughout the quarter.

The PUCSL has invited written submissions from stakeholders on the proposed tariff revision and the underlying cost components by 5 November. An oral consultation will also be held at the Bandaranaike Memorial International Conference Hall (BMICH) in Colombo on the same day from 9 a.m.

The fourth-quarter tariff review is being conducted under the quarterly tariff determination requirements of the Sri Lanka Electricity Act No. 36 of 2024, as amended. No final tariff decision has yet been announced.

title: Ceylon Literary and Arts Festival hosts inaugural London Edition | Daily FT
summary:

Ceylon Literary and Arts Festival Founder Ajai Vir Singh (left) and Co-Founder Fazeena Rajabdeen

The Ceylon Literary and Arts Festival (CLAF), which has focused on creating an influential arts and culture platform for Sri Lanka while profiling the island through its creative industries, is now preparing for its fourth edition. It has gained traction in a short time, guided by clear objectives that create meaningful opportunities for young people through its four pillars: literature, art, music and film.

Enhancing Sri Lanka’s soft power is one of the platform’s key missions, alongside engaging young people in these creative streams.

Sri Lanka’s stories and the writers who tell them took centre stage in London as CLAF held its London Edition to World Travel Market (WTM) on 4 November. Presented by Sri Lanka Tourism, the event invited international audiences to discover the island through literature, ideas and conversation.

Ceylon Literary and Arts Festival Founder Ajai Vir Singh said: “The London Edition is an important step as we expand our platform’s footprint beyond Sri Lanka, and it also strengthens Sri Lanka’s soft power. Bringing the festival to London alongside Sri Lanka Tourism is a key strategic goal in attracting the right travellers to the country. Arts and culture are an important medium for engaging a wider international audience.”

The list of speakers included Shrabani Basu, author of Victoria & Abdul, which was adapted into a film starring Judi Dench; Booker-shortlisted novelist Romesh Gunasekera; Louise Doughty, whose fiction has been adapted for BBC One and ITV; comic novelist Ashok Ferrey; and economist Razeen Sally, author of Return to Sri Lanka. Their work spans history, fiction, humour and economics.

Ceylon Literary and Arts Festival Co-founder Fazeena Rajabdeen said: “Culture is one of the most powerful ways a country can introduce itself. After four years of building a festival with Sri Lankan voices at its heart, we wanted to take those voices to the world, starting with London.” 

Following a welcome address by Ajai Vir Singh, the afternoon unfolded across three conversations. In Sri Lanka through the Eyes of Others, Romesh Gunasekera and Razeen Sally will be joined by moderator Ashok Ferrey; One Tear of Love brings together Louise Doughty and Ashok Ferrey; and in Tales from the Empire, Shrabani Basu was in conversation with Ashok Ferrey.

The London Edition also introduced the festival’s fourth edition, taking place in Colombo from 22 to 24 January 2027, and encouraged travel professionals to consider literature and the arts as reasons to visit Sri Lanka. The festival will bring together writers, artists, musicians and filmmakers from Sri Lanka and around the world across its four pillars of literature, art, music and film, with young and emerging Sri Lankan creatives at its heart. The full line-up, venues and ticketing details will be announced in the coming weeks.

At district level, Colombo recorded the highest poverty line at Rs. 19,136, followed by Gampaha at Rs. 19,037 and Kalutara at Rs. 18,624. Nuwara Eliya had the lowest figure at Rs. 16,558, followed by Monaragala at Rs. 16,965.

title: IMF questions lower excise on imported liquor | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 5 November 2026 06:46
-     - 17

Sri Lanka subjects imported alcoholic beverages to a lower fixed excise rate per litre than domestically produced alcohol, a treatment the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said should be integrated into the Medium-Term Revenue Strategy (MTRS) policy and administration agenda.

“This differential treatment is unusual, as imported and domestically produced excise goods are typically subject to equivalent excise rates to protect revenue, support neutrality, and reduce opportunities for arbitrage,” the IMF said in its Revenue Administration Diagnostic, recommending an assessment of a more neutral rate basis supported by stronger border controls, stamp verification, production monitoring and market surveillance.

Responsibility for excise administration is split across several institutions. Sri Lanka Excise (SLE) is responsible for alcohol, beedis and excise on tobacco leaf; Sri Lanka Customs (SLC) handles border controls over imported alcohol and administers excise on tobacco products, vehicles and sugary soft drinks; and excise on petroleum products is managed by the Ceylon Petroleum Corporation. The IMF said this allocation differs from common international practice and called for a time-bound review of closer integration with SLC, including a possible Customs and Excise model, while ensuring immediate action on alcohol, beedi, stamp and market controls is not delayed.

The report identified an urgent vendor-transition risk in the alcohol security-sticker regime. The contract with Madras Security Printers expires in January 2027, and SLE has advised that bids for the next vendor have been opened. Licensed liquor production reached 43.3 million absolute litres in 2022 following the introduction of the security-sticker system, declined to 35.1 million in 2023 and 35.3 million in 2024, and recovered to 40.4 million in 2025, which SLE attributes primarily to a substantial reduction in illegal products. Production totalled 20.8 million absolute litres through 30 June, 2026.

SLE does not consider a previously cited estimate that illicit alcohol accounts for approximately 40% of the market sufficiently reliable, and intends to procure a research study by a government university approved by the University Grants Commission; the IMF accordingly did not quantify a potential revenue loss. “Revenue losses from illicit or under-declared excise goods therefore reduce both excise and VAT collections, creating a cascading revenue effect that is larger than the excise loss alone,” it noted.

Staffing levels are low. SLE reported actual staffing of 1,140 against an approved cadre of 1,649 as at 31 December, 2025, leaving 509 vacancies, with staff also assigned to non-revenue functions including illegal narcotics control. The Revenue Administration System for the Excise Department (RASED), expected to include 15 modules, had its first module planned for launch in October 2026, with full implementation expected by 2028. Two liquor manufacturing facilities are currently fully automated.

“Resident officers stationed at producer premises are resource-intensive and can become routine, reducing their effectiveness as a control mechanism over time,” the report said, recommending they be gradually replaced by proportionate systems-based controls as RASED becomes operational, while safeguarding legitimate traditional manufacturing practices.

title: Govt. relaxes TIN requirements for bank accounts, vehicle licence renewals | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 5 November 2026 06:46
-     - 17

The Finance Ministry yesterday clarified that individuals can open bank accounts and renew motor vehicle revenue licences without producing a Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN) certificate, following special arrangements to prevent disruptions to the two services.

Under the arrangements announced jointly with the Inland Revenue Department and the Registrar of Motor Vehicles, applicants who already have a TIN can provide the number, while those yet to register can submit their National Identity Card number, name, address, telephone number and email address.

 The relevant institutions will facilitate TIN registration or obtain the number using the information provided.

The Ministry said these services should not be delayed or refused solely because applicants cannot produce a TIN certificate.

The clarification follows the introduction, from 1 November, of a requirement to submit TIN certificates for eight specified transactions. Apart from opening bank or financial institution accounts and renewing vehicle revenue licences, the requirement applies to obtaining credit cards, building plan approvals, vehicle registration, land registration, business registration and transfers of company shares. The special arrangements apply only to the first two transactions, with certificates required for the remaining six.

The Ministry also confirmed that printed and electronic TIN certificates are equally valid, with no requirement for official signatures, seals, stamps or certified copies.

While all resident individuals aged 18 and above are legally required to obtain a TIN, the Ministry stressed that registration does not automatically create an income tax liability. Tax becomes payable only when annual income exceeds the prescribed threshold of Rs. 1.8 million.

Individuals who do not immediately need a TIN have been advised to defer registration until congestion at the Inland Revenue Department and its online system eases.

title: Democrats seize control of Congress in rebuke to Trump | Daily FT

Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed speaks after winning the State’s US Senate race and making history

The Democratic Party has wrested control of both chambers of the US Congress from Republicans in a sweeping electoral victory, delivering a major rebuke to President Donald Trump and his political agenda.

The party secured majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate, making significant gains in traditionally Republican strongholds, including Texas, South Carolina and Kansas. Kansas had not elected a Democrat to the Senate in almost a century. The Democrats took the House with 228 seats against 139 to Republicans, and secured 54 Senate seats against 44 to Republicans.

The results also delivered a breakthrough for progressive Democrats, with Abdul El-Sayed winning the Michigan Senate race to become the first Muslim to serve in the US Senate.

Trump acknowledged that the war with Iran had contributed to the Republican defeat, as rising fuel prices and broader inflation added to voter concerns over the administration’s policies.

The scale of the Democratic gains marked a significant shift in the balance of power in Washington, handing the party control of Congress and presenting a major political setback for the President.

title: Sri Lanka export excellence initiative supports SMEs to scale globally | Daily FT

The Sri Lanka Export Development Board (EDB), in collaboration with the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and the European Union (EU), successfully conducted the final pitching event of batch III of ExpoScaleUp, designed to help Sri Lankan SMEs become more competitive and expand into global markets. Supported through the EU’s regional Accelerating Climate Smart and Inclusive Infrastructure in South Asia (ACSIIS) initiative under the EU Global Gateway Strategy, ExpoScaleUp is part of the Sri Lanka Export Excellence Initiative (SLEEI), a flagship program aimed at strengthening SME export readiness, market access and long-term competitiveness.

Through ExpoScaleUp III, 25 Sri Lankan SMEs developed export market plans to sharpen their strategies and position their businesses for international growth. The program concluded with a pitching event, where participants presented their business potential and pathways to new markets before a panel of experts.

In his opening address, EDB Chairman Mangala Wijesinghe, highlighted the importance of SMEs in strengthening Sri Lanka’s export sector and expanding the country’s presence in international markets. He also acknowledged the collaborative efforts of IFC and the European Union in supporting Sri Lankan enterprises through initiatives aimed at enhancing their capabilities and export competitiveness.

Speaking at the event, IFC South Asia Manager-Country Advisory and Economics Gregory Smith, emphasised that helping SMEs are central to Sri Lanka’s economy, and helping them compete globally is key to unlocking Sri Lanka’s growth, creating jobs and strengthening economic resilience. 

He noted that IFC has long provided SMEs with finance and expertise to help SMEs strengthen their businesses and enter new markets. This partnership builds on that foundation, helping more Sri Lankan businesses develop the capabilities and connections they need to compete and grow globally.”

Delegation of the EU to Sri Lanka and the Maldives Head of Partnerships Virginie Lafleur-Tighe said, “The EU is proud to support the ExpoScaleUp program as part of our broader partnership with Sri Lanka under the ACSIIS regional program. This initiative reflects our shared commitment to strengthening the competitiveness of SMEs by helping them become more export-ready, more sustainable, and better equipped to meet evolving market standards. By linking private sector development with climate action, and by working closely with partners such as IFC and the EDB, we are contributing to a more resilient, inclusive, and future-ready export ecosystem in Sri Lanka.”

Participating SMEs represented a diverse range of sectors, including spices and concentrates, processed food and beverages, coconut-based products, gifts and handicrafts, ICT/BPO, and herbal cosmetics. 

Ten SMEs were recognised for the best Export Market Plans, highlighting their efforts to develop structured market-entry strategies and identify opportunities for sustainable export growth. Selected SMEs will have the opportunity to advance to ExpoConnect, the program’s next stage, focused on market access, trade facilitation, and targeted matchmaking with international buyers. 

Nearly 750 SMEs across Sri Lanka have benefited from the SLEEI program through regional awareness sessions and business clinics. The initiative highlights the commitment of the EDB, IFC and the European Union to helping Sri Lankan SMEs compete globally.

Sri Lanka will set up a sovereign-backed fund of funds for startups, develop a regulatory framework for virtual assets and virtual asset service providers, and expand telecom coverage to over 99% of the population, Deputy Minister of Digital Economy Eng. Eranga Weeraratne said.

He made the remarks at the recent Sri Lanka FinTech Festival 2026 in Colombo, where he outlined a broader push to accelerate digital adoption and position the country as a regional fintech hub.

Weeraratne said Sri Lanka may be a few years behind other regional countries in digital payment and fintech adoption, but said the country has the necessary ingredients to move faster, including a strong IT talent pool, an established IT industry, a heavily banked population, high literacy and government commitment to digital transformation.

He said the Government’s ambition is to move Sri Lanka from a cash-heavy society towards a cash-light, digitally enabled economy, while also helping local IT and fintech companies export solutions to global markets.

“We are setting up a fund of funds, a sovereign fund, for investing in our startups, and we are inviting other international and local funds to contribute,” he said.

The fund is expected to provide matching capital for startups, while the Government works with local and international fund managers to create the policies and documentation needed to connect Sri Lankan entrepreneurs with global capital.

Weeraratne also said work is under way on regulations for virtual assets and virtual asset service providers, a move intended to give clarity to businesses and investors and allow local firms to innovate in the sector.

On digital payments, he said the Government will push QR-based payments through promotions, incentives and support for devices, aiming to shift both consumers and merchants away from cash.

He said banks should develop financial products linked to digital payment usage, as transaction records can help small merchants demonstrate business performance and creditworthiness.

“Digital payment histories can become a new form of collateral for SMEs,” he said.

The Deputy Minister also said telecom coverage, currently around 94–95% of the population, will be expanded beyond 99% within the next two to three years, with investment and support from partners including the Asian Development Bank.

To build trust in digital services, the Government plans to establish a cybersecurity regulatory authority under forthcoming legislation and invest in advanced security operations centres to protect public and private digital infrastructure.

Weeraratne said interoperability, open systems and low-code tools will be key to allowing new services to be built on national platforms and helping Sri Lankan fintech firms export solutions.

However, Central Bank Governor Dr. Nandalal Weerasinghe cautioned that virtual assets cannot be used for payments between residents under Sri Lanka’s current legal framework.

“This position is important in preventing the substitution of the Sri Lankan rupee in domestic transactions and in safeguarding the country’s monetary sovereignty,” he said.

Delivering the keynote on ‘The Future of FinTech,’ Weerasinghe said Sri Lanka’s post-crisis recovery has created the foundation for growth, but the next phase must focus on productivity, investment, employment and innovation.

“Stability is not the destination; it is the foundation upon which sustainable growth must be built,” he said.

He said fintech can help mobilise savings, channel capital to productive investment, reduce transaction costs and improve financial inclusion, particularly for small businesses and underserved communities.

Sri Lanka already has digital banking, mobile and internet banking, payment cards, digital payment applications and interoperable national payment infrastructure through LankaPay, he noted.

Looking ahead, the Governor identified open and interoperable financial services, digital identity, data-driven lending, cross-border payment connectivity and digital investment services as key growth areas.

He also warned that fintech brings risks, including cyberattacks, operational disruptions, fraud, data breaches, inadequate consumer disclosures, excessive leverage and concentration of critical services among technology providers.

“We must strike the right balance: encouraging competition and innovation while ensuring effective supervision, sound risk management and strong consumer protection,” Weerasinghe said.

He reiterated that the Central Bank remains open to innovation and pointed to its FinTech Regulatory Sandbox as a controlled environment for testing eligible financial solutions.

FinTech Forum Sri Lanka Chairman Channa de Silva said the theme of this year’s festival was much more than a tagline.

“It highlights the opportunity in front of us, at an organisation and a national level. Bringing together innovators, financial institutions, policymakers and global partners, we showcased Sri Lanka’s fintech capabilities, opened doors to attract investment and talent, and created pathways for local solutions to scale internationally,” he said.

“Our ultimate ambition is to turn collaboration into lasting economic value for the country and position Sri Lanka as a fintech hub in the regional fintech landscape.”

The festival served as a showcase of Sri Lanka’s existing digital-payment infrastructure, connecting the local ecosystem with regional and international financial developments. Sessions highlighted how the country has already built essential digital rails and how these platforms can support cross-border transactions, investment, regional market access and Sri Lanka’s ambition to emerge as a digital economy hub in Asia.

The Sri Lanka FinTech Festival 2026, organised by FinTech Forum Sri Lanka in collaboration with the Digital Economy Ministry and powered by Visa, was held from 2 to 3 November at Shangri-La Colombo under the theme ‘Building Capacity, Creating Opportunities and Scaling Sri Lanka’s Digital Future.’

The festival brought together policymakers, regulators, banks, non-bank financial institutions, technology firms, investors, entrepreneurs, SMEs and tourism-sector stakeholders to discuss the future of digital finance and showcase Sri Lanka’s digital financial services capabilities.

The two-day event included the FinTech Expo conference, featuring exhibition floors, keynotes and panel discussions, and concluded with FinTech Night and the FinTech Awards 2026, which recognised contributors to Sri Lanka’s fintech ecosystem.

title: Northern Exporters Forum 2027: Connecting local production with global markets | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 5 November 2026 05:47
-     - 15

By Raj Sivanathan

The Northern Exporters Forum 2027 has been officially launched as an important initiative to connect the Northern Province’s productive capacity and natural resources with international markets.

The forum will be held on 20 and 21 January 2027 at the Thiruvalluvar Cultural Centre in Jaffna. Its official launch and programme briefing took place on 29 October 2026 at the Northern Province Governor’s Secretariat, under the leadership of Governor N. Vethanayahan.

The Governor said the forum would support the goal of increasing the Northern Province’s contribution to Sri Lanka’s gross domestic product from 4.5 per cent to 10 per cent. He emphasised the importance of expanding production, adding value, reaching new markets and attracting investment. The province has considerable potential in agriculture, fisheries, palmyrah-based products, handicrafts, information technology, tourism and cultural industries.

From investment to export growth

Following the investment summit organised in the Northern Province this year, the Management Club of Sri Lanka’s decision to hold an exporters’ forum represents a useful next step in supporting the region’s economic development. Attracting investment is important, but so is helping local products reach wider markets and creating opportunities to sell them.

The forum aims to introduce goods produced and services offered in the Northern Province to overseas markets, while strengthening the capabilities of small and medium-sized enterprises preparing to export.

The sectors expected to feature include agriculture and processed foods, palmyrah-based products, seafood, handloom and handicrafts, information technology, renewable energy, small industries, wellness products, traditional medicine, medical equipment, tourism and cultural industries.

Alongside stronger links with the Indian market, the Northern Province can create new opportunities for local producers by engaging diaspora business networks in the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia and other countries. The diaspora’s knowledge, connections and investment capacity can help build links between local producers and overseas buyers.

Business connections and export readiness

The two-day forum will include seminars, discussions, an exhibition of products and services, presentations by businesses and direct business meetings.

The organisers aim to facilitate at least 50 to 75 business meetings and attract between 75 and 100 qualified buyers. These meetings will give Northern producers the opportunity to discuss product quality, pricing, supply capacity and export potential directly with buyers.

Guidance will also be provided on international market information, overseas trade regulations, quality certifications, trade finance, risk management, transportation and supply-chain arrangements. As part of the preparations, workshops were held on 3 and 4 November.

The success of the forum should not be measured only by the number of organisations attending. Its long-term value will depend on the business agreements that follow, ongoing buyer relationships, stronger production capacity and sustainable export earnings.

A move to simplify investment procedures

A tripartite agreement was signed at the meeting to advance an online initiative aimed at reducing the difficulties investors face when seeking approvals from multiple government departments.

The agreement was signed by Northern Province Governor N. Vethanayahan, Vavuniya University Vice-Chancellor Arputharajah and Management Club of Sri Lanka Project Chairman Kaushal Rajapaksa. The initiative is intended to coordinate investors’ engagement with relevant departments and institutions, and make it easier to obtain the information they need.

A programme to establish school gardens in all five districts of the Northern Province was also introduced at the event. In the first phase, one school from each district will be selected. The programme is planned to continue through the Lions Club.

Cooperation and continuity are essential

The Management Club of Sri Lanka is organising the forum, with the Ministry of Industry and Entrepreneurship Development providing leadership and support. The Consulate General of India in Jaffna is a key cooperation partner. The Export Development Board, National Chamber of Exporters, National Enterprise Development Authority and Industrial Development Board are also involved as partners. Vavuniya University will serve as the regional project management unit.

Consul General of India Sai Murali, who attended the meeting, noted that useful lessons could be shared from similar initiatives previously undertaken in India. Such exchanges could help strengthen the export readiness of local producers.

The Northern Exporters Forum 2027 has the potential to provide an important platform for showcasing the province’s productive capacity. For that opportunity to translate into lasting economic benefits, producers will need continued practical support before and after the forum—including market information, access to finance and technical assistance, quality improvements and transport facilities. With sustained cooperation, products from the Northern Province can secure a lasting place in domestic and international markets.

title: CHOGM 2026 opens with drive to unlock prosperity for Commonwealth’s 2.7 billion people | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 5 November 2026 06:55
-     - 7

Head of the Commonwealth Charles III

The 2026 Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) opened in Antigua and Barbuda on Tuesday with a drive for bold partnerships between governments and businesses to unlock prosperity for the Commonwealth’s 2.7 billion people. 

Charles III, Head of the Commonwealth, joined leaders from across the Commonwealth at the official Opening Ceremony on 3 November 2026 in St. John’s, where they were welcomed with a vibrant performance and dance, celebrating Antiguan and Barbudan culture and history. 

The ceremony marked the start of leaders’ deliberations under the theme ‘Accelerating Partnerships and Investment for a Prosperous Commonwealth’.  

This is the first CHOGM under the leadership of Commonwealth Secretary-General Hon Shirley Botchwey. It will also be the first time Heads of Government engage directly at CHOGM with business leaders, investors, heads of international financial institutions and philanthropists. Their focus will be on mobilising partnerships and investment in scalable projects that will tangibly respond to member country needs, including in areas of skills-building, climate finance and green energy.

‘Unparalleled opportunity’ 

In his remarks, the King said: “All around us, trust between nations is under critical strain, as international norms and systems are tested to their limits. Brutal conflict stalks our world, destroying lives and casting long shadows across the globe. Technology is transforming our societies and our economies at dizzying speed, with little certainty about where it might lead us. 

“As I have consistently tried to emphasise, climate change is no longer just a terrifying prospect, but a catastrophic reality which threatens our very way of life… And in each of our countries, for too many people, the opportunity to fulfil their own potential lies far beyond their reach.  

 “Each of these is a challenge of the highest order. Together, they comprise the crisis of our time. The Commonwealth cannot provide all of the solutions. It does, however, offer an unparalleled opportunity to work together – across our societies and our economies, through our businesses, our institutions and our communities. It allows us to draw on the collective ingenuity of a third of humanity to address the challenges confronting us all.” 

Echoing The King’s remarks, Secretary-General Botchwey said the world today is “sorely in need of the Commonwealth spirit of always finding a way”. 

“Together with our hosts, and our member countries, we have remade this CHOGM as a summit of action. Our goal is to build a new model of partnership and cooperation that is capable of responding to the scale of challenge we face; to avoid the mistakes of the past by making our collective interest the sum of our individual national interest. It is a success strategy that requires a mindset change, including discarding the old division of labour between states and business.” 

She said that strategy is already taking shape through new initiatives to mobilise investment, boost intra-Commonwealth trade, upskill young people and expand renewable energy. 

Addressing the Heads of Government, the Secretary-General said: “Our people will judge this meeting by what it delivers for them. Each of you brings the authority to act on behalf of your country. Together, you can deliver for a third of humanity. I urge you to seize this chance to build resilience and shared prosperity together.”

A consequential CHOGM 

Prime Minister of Antigua and Barbuda Gaston Browne described the meeting as a “consequential CHOGM”, pointing to early results including US$200 million mobilised through the Nature Initiative and US$1.3 billion announced through the Global Eye Health Summit.  

Prime Minister Browne, who takes over from Samoa as Commonwealth Chair-in-Office said: “We cannot, through the Commonwealth alone, eliminate the divisions that confront our world. But we can refuse to allow those divisions to determine the limits of our ambition or diminish the hopes of our people. Let history remember that, at this moment of global uncertainty, we chose cooperation over division, solidarity over indifference, and action over empty promises. Let ours be a Commonwealth that gives every member a voice, every young person a horizon of opportunity, and every nation a fair chance to prosper. A Commonwealth that stands as a force for good, a conscience in the international community and a stabilising influence in an unsettled world. That is the Commonwealth our people deserve.” 

During this summit, Heads of Government and business leaders are meeting in two dedicated sessions to mobilise finance for an over $52 billion pipeline of investment-ready projects from 28 developing Commonwealth countries.  

Leaders will also consider a new Commonwealth work programme to remove barriers to intra-Commonwealth trade; a common approach to sustainable debt and concessional finance that better reflects vulnerability; and a plan to carry the investment agenda forward in 2027.  

With 60 per cent of Commonwealth citizens under the age of 30, leaders will discuss how to expand education, skills and entrepreneurship opportunities for young people. Discussions will also cover building democratic resilience, accelerating climate action and responding to the particular challenges facing small states.

Climate pressure  

Deputy Prime Minister Mulipola Anarosa Ale-Molio’o of Samoa, speaking as outgoing Commonwealth Chair-in-Office, highlighted the growing pressure of climate change on small and vulnerable states. 

“The world is already pushing past the critical 1.5°C degree threshold. Many nations and communities are facing permanent losses, but overshoot must not become an excuse for delayed admission or inaction, the Commonwealth must hear the calls from the recent Pacific Pre-COP31 discussions in Fiji and Tuvalu.  

“Accessible and predictable climate finance is the bridge between ambition and action. No nation should have to borrow its way out of a crisis it did so little to create.” 

The CHOGM executive sessions will culminate in the Leaders’ Retreat, which gives Heads of Government an opportunity to have frank discussions in an informal setting. 

Alongside the summit, Youth, Women’s, People’s and Business Forums are being held to bring voices from across the Commonwealth into the meeting, with additional events focused on blue finance, eye health, governance and democracy, and sport for development. 

By the close of CHOGM, leaders are expected to issue a communiqué setting out agreed priorities and commitments to build resilience and expand opportunities for people across the Commonwealth’s 56 member countries.

title: Tragedy of SLFP tradition | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 5 November 2026 05:06
-     - 34

Chandrika’s contributions to the two-party system

Mahinda Rajapaksa: Highest achiever in the SLFP tradition

Ranil who was never elected President by the citizenry, was appointed to that post by Gotabaya Rajapaksa and endorsed by the SLPP—reloading Chandrika’s 2015 ‘hybrid’. Ranil’s economic stabilisation/adjustment ‘shock therapy’ (2022-2024) further crunched the SLPP’s base after Gotabaya’s ‘fertiliser shock’ had shrunk it (2019-2022). SLPP voters shifted to the JVP-NPP

The phrase “The Children of ’56” coined by Mervyn de Silva in 1973 (Sri Lanka: The End of Welfare Politics, South Asian Review, UK, 1973), recorded as such in the published doctoral thesis of Prof. Gamini Samaranayake, was plagiarised and popularised in Sinhala by the founding ‘philosopher’ of Jathika Chinthanaya.

I am literally a child of ’56. That was the year Ceylon/Sri Lanka’s two-party system was born with the replacement in power of the dominant postcolonial party the UNP, commencing the alternation in power of two democratic parties/coalitions, two decades before India passed that landmark of political development. 2026 is the 70th anniversary year of the birth of the island’s two-party system.

The shocking success of the JVP, leaping from 3 seats and 3% to the Presidency and a 2/3rds majority in Parliament was possible only because of the crisis of the two-party system and the two main political traditions:

The UNP and its SJB successor.

The SLFP and its SLPP successor.

The SLFP had been the most successful political party in the country. Under two leaders, Chandrika Bandaranaike Kumaratunga and Mahinda Rajapaksa, it led the country for two decades uninterruptedly from 1994 to 2014.

Before 1994 and CBK, the SLFP led by Sirimavo Bandaranaike had been in the Opposition for 17 years.

The SLFP suffered two crashes:

From the country’s first-ever Government with a 2/3rds majority in Parliament (1970) to a 17-year exile from Government.

From 1994-2014 to the current period.

Maithripala Senanayake: Potential winning-card the SLFP never played

Maithripala Senanayake

When the SLFP-led coalition Government’s popularity was  free-falling with the OPEC oil price shock (1973), its economic policy was criticised imprecisely as ‘too far to the left’, which meant in reality, too far in the direction of ‘statism’ and ‘self-sufficiency’. Sirimavo Bandaranaike attempted to course-correct by removing Dr. NM Perera and the LSSP from the Government and appointing Felix Dias Bandaranaike as Finance Minister. He was accurately perceived as ‘too far to the authoritarian right’, and further jeopardised the centre-left SLFP and the constricted coalition (SLFP-CPSL).

The SLFP crashed to its worst defeat with the TULF scoring more seats in the 1977 parliament.  The party’s crisis was compounded by the dismal showing of its candidate Hector Kobbekaduwa at the Presidential election of October 1982 against incumbent JR Jayewardene.

But there was one option which if exercised could have mitigated the crisis of the UF coalition in the 1970s, narrowed the margin between the Jayewardene UNP and the SLFP candidate in October 1982, and shortened the SLFP’s 17-year spell of defeat.

The SLFP had within its topmost ranks a figure who was seen simultaneously as a moderate democrat in economics and governance, but also a progressive who enjoyed the support of the LSSP- CPSL and the USSR. That was the SLFP’s Deputy Leader and the UF Government’s Deputy Prime Minister who acted for Madam Bandaranaike when she was overseas: Maithripala Senanayake of Anuradhapura, an electorally unbeaten political giant from the rural Sinhala heartland who had also studied Tamil and was married to a journalist who was an ethnic Tamil.

Had Maithripala Senanayake been given a fair chance, it could have reduced the extent of (but not entirely avoided) the swing to the UNP in 1977 and given JR a run for his money in October 1982.

After decades of marginalisation by the Ratwatte-Bandaranaikes, a bitterly disappointed Maithripala Senanayake finally defected to JR Jayewardene, rather like Philip Gunawardena did to Dudley Senanayake.

Squandered chances

It took almost two decades from the 1977 debacle for the SLFP to win under Chandrika Bandaranaike Kumaratunga.

No President since JR Jayewardene had the chances and options of CBK as president but she consistently ignored them in favour of unrealistic, irrational, irresponsible experimentation.

After the Tigers returned unilaterally to war in 1995 despite her offer of an overgenerous political package, she could have leveraged the  goodwill and support she enjoyed from India, implemented the Indo-Sri Lanka Accord and the 13th Amendment, appointing an interim administration for the territory (as Douglas Devananda urged). Instead, she continued to chase in 1997, in wartime, the mirage of a political package with the LTTE which she now publicly divulges as federalism.

Despite the fact that an LTTE suicide bomber tried to kill her at an election rally in 1999, she pursued a Norwegian-facilitated peace effort. When ‘9/11’ provided the perfect opening  for widespread global support to win the war and follow-up with devolution, she continued dogmatically with the one-sided Norwegian effort.

The rise of the extremist ultranationalist Sinhala new right ancestor of the BBS, led at the time by Champika Ranawake, was an outcome—as was the dramatic ascendancy of the JVP.

Whitewashing the JVP

The JVP was crushed and decapitated in November 1989, the very year after it assassinated Vijaya Kumaratunga by shooting him in the face on his doorstep. At the time the JVP didn’t disclaim the  brutal killing despite the huge public opinion backlash. Instead, on the day of Vijaya’s funeral, the JVP’s front organisation-cum-military wing the DJV (precursor of today’s NPP or JJB) distributed an openly justificatory leaflet entitled ‘Vijaya Yavvey Aiy?’ which in translation meant ‘Why Was Vijaya Despatched?’ It called him a CIA agent, among other things.

The JVP’s catapulting to the Presidency and huge preponderance in Parliament in 2024 was mightily assisted by the laundering through a Presidential Commission appointed by President Chandrika Bandaranaike Kumaratunga of the stain of the delegitimising sin of Vijaya Kumaratunga’s cruel murder. She had viciously and irrationally accused President Premadasa (at the time, Prime Minister) and not Wijeweera’s JVP of murdering her husband and father of her two children. This despite the arrest and long, detailed confession by the gunman tasked and trained by the JVP for this and a series of other assassinations.

Chandrika’s accusation was unethical because Premadasa who had been blown up by a Tiger suicide bomber had no way to defend himself. It was irrational because if Vijaya ran for the Presidency as he had announced, it would have split more votes from Mrs. Bandaranaike and helped Premadasa far more than Vijaya’s successor Ossie Abeygoonesekara’s candidacy did in 1988.

Betrayal 2005

The worst damage to the SLFP came at the tail-end of her term when she went against the counsel of her brilliant Foreign Minister Lakshman Kadirgamar, and persisted in the project of a post-tsunami power-sharing mechanism (PTOMS) with the Tigers. That ‘Munich’-type betrayal was thwarted on two fronts:

The US Government, which emphasised that it was prevented by Congress from contributing funds to any structure involving a designated terrorist organisation. I was at the US Ambassador Jeff Lunstead’s when Asst Secretary of State Christina Roca told that upfront to Ambassador Jayantha Dhanapala, CBK’s chief negotiator with the LTTE over the PTOMS.

The Supreme Court of Sri Lanka which froze the vital middle tier of the mechanism located in the Wanni since it was inaccessible to the Sri Lankan State.

Fortunately for the SLFP, its founding father (CBK’s father) SWRD Bandaranaike had a firm partner from the South when he began his independent political journey: DA Rajapaksa, whose son was the popular Prime Minister Mahinda Rajapaksa, a populist rebel known to dissent from the ‘CBK line’.

Out of options, CBK grudgingly nominated Mahinda who won the 2005 Presidential election—but not before she had gouged a wound that has never healed in the SLFP.

I was a visiting Adjunct Professor at the School of Advanced International Studies (SAIS) of Johns Hopkins University in Washington DC in Fall 2005 when CBK came to town accompanied by Ambassador Dhanapala. The purpose of her visit was to lobby in support of his bid for the post of UN Secretary-General. Prof. Walter Anderson who headed the South Asia program at SAIS, called me into his office and told me that Sri Lanka’s President had hosted a dinner the previous night which he had attended, and rolled-out a view quite contrary to that which I had said on the record at Georgetown’s Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) on a panel with Ambassador Bernard Gunatilleke and Gajan Ponnambalam, Chaired by Ambassador Teresita Schaeffer. Neil de Votta and Asoka Bandarage participated, Ravinatha Aryasinha was present, TamilNet carried a report.

I predicted that:

Prabhakaran would boycott the Presidential Election because he discouraged ‘Eelam Tamil’ participation in a Sri Lankan election.

Mahinda Rajapaksa would win the Presidency.

The Tigers would launch the Final War.

Mahinda would defeat them.

The US and India should support the Sri Lankan State against the Tigers, and endeavour to shape the postwar outcome in the direction of implementing existing devolution.

Following my presentation, Steve Ghitelman who headed the South Asia desk of the US State Department’s prestigious research wing, the INR, came up and invited me to speak on the upcoming election and the peace process to an inter-agency audience convened by/at the State Dept, which I did.

Prof. Walter Anderson told me that President Kumaratunga had informed them at dinner that she would support Opposition candidate Ranil Wickremesinghe at the election, he would win, Mahinda would lose, and she and Ranil together would offer Prabhakaran a federal solution, ushering in peace.

Knowing  CBK to be a lady of her word, I promptly pressed the ejector-button on my Washington gig, returned to Colombo and leaped into the election campaign, appearing on TV in support of Mahinda.

Mahinda Rajapaksa had to contest with a divided SLFP, his old friend Anura Bandaranaike (and even Sarath Amunugama) against him. After Mahinda won, Mangala Samaraweera tried to stall his assumption of SLFP leadership. MR plugged the gap with the support of his family ‘clan’, the ultranationalist Hela Urumaya, and the JVP. Mahinda had been until then, an opponent of an SLFP-JVP alliance which he prophesied would siphon-off SLFP votes to the JVP someday.

The UNP was wrecked by Ranil, the SLFP by Chandrika, the SLPP by Gotabaya. That’s how and why AKD and the JVP  prevailed

Betrayal 2015

Chandrika Kumaratunga’s role in forming a coalition between a breakaway faction of the SLFP led by Maithripala Sirisena and the UNP against the MR Presidency would’ve been politically legitimate in the aftermath of Bharatha Lakshman Premachandra’s killing, except she forged a coalition which she knew from experience was unsustainable.

CBK’s experiment in political cohabitation with Ranil Wickremesinghe who was Prime Minister in 2001-2003, ended because she simply had to fire him, go for an election and defeat him. No cohabitation between SLFP and UNP was sustainable so long as Ranil, with his neoliberal and abjectly pro-Western views, was partner.

An SLFP-UNP bloc was sustainable only as a centrist coalition, feasible if the UNP was represented by a liberal-centrist whose views were compatible with the SLFP’s. Chandrika could have insisted on Karu Jayasuriya as the dissident SLFP’s partner. A Maithri-Karu convergence would have been sustainable.

Instead, CBK visited the UNP headquarters Siri Kotha and stitched together a Sirisena-Wickremesinghe equation. In 2015 she put into practice the plan she had divulged in Washington DC in Autumn 2005.

The SLFP’s base and (therefore) most of the SLFP parliamentary group couldn’t be won over to the Yahapalanaya agenda driven by Ranil’s UNP which didn’t shift to the centre but remained on the neoliberal right.

Two devastating outcomes issued from CBK’s 2015 move:

1. The SLFP shattered, with the overwhelming majority remaining loyal to Mahinda Rajapaksa and launching the SLPP.

2. The infant breakaway SLPP crushingly defeated the governing UNP of Prime Minister Ranil Wickremasinghe, reducing it to 20% of the vote at the Feb 2018 Local Government election.

Desperate to save the SLFP from terminal erosion by alignment with Ranil’s UNP, President Sirisena re-linked in late-2018 with Mahinda Rajapaksa who had retained the bulk of the SLFP’s vote-base. This ‘52-day experiment’ was thwarted by the decision of the Supreme Court which predictably ruled-out a dissolution and snap election. In conversations from Moscow with Mahinda Rajapaksa and President Sirisena, I had cautioned that a snap election was highly improbable, and urged a non-binding Referendum instead.

The elated, delusional UNP thought that the next election was in the bag. The reality was that the UNP never emerged from the 20% trough of February 2018—nor did or has its derivative/successor, the SJB.

The SLPP swept the board in 2019, but that led to another disaster because it was not Mahinda Rajapaksa who was candidate. Mahinda had blundered in attempting a third term, with a colluding CJ dismissing as unnecessary a referendum to change the constitutional two-term limit—and lost the gamble (2015). The Yahapalanaya Government (2015-2019) then unfairly banned Mahinda from running for even a non-consecutive third term, which had it existed in Brazil would have prevented Lula being re-elected.

The far-right Gotabaya Rajapaksa candidacy and constituency issued from:

The necessity which arose with the gap left by the ban on MR’s candidacy.

The shift in the balance of the SLFP and its partners, strengthening the ultranationalist element when Chandrika divided it in 2005 in her attempt to sabotage Mahinda.

The catastrophic Gotabaya Presidency was overthrown by the Sri Lankan citizens led by the university students and youth.

Chandrika’s whitewashing of the JVP’s murder of her husband; appeasement of the LTTE; overlong dalliance with the hardly-neutral Norwegians; attempts to federalise the Sri Lankan State; indecisiveness in fighting the war; ignoring Lakshman Kadirgamar’s reluctance about the PTOMS; tilt to Ranil over Mahinda in 2005; midwifery of the Yahapalanaya bipartisan coalition with Ranil’s UNP; set off a chain reaction which exploded BOTH the SLFP and the UNP, the twin pillars of Sri Lankan democracy, at their bases—thereby creating the systemic void the JVP filled.

The SLFP created by SWRD Bandaranaike breaking away from the UNP, was realigned by Chandrika with the UNP under its most neoliberal leader, ending the two-party system as we knew it from 1951, making inevitable the rise of new forces to fill the space, play the role.

Post-2019

Instead of voting for their own Dullas Alahapperuma at the Parliamentary selection of the President in 2022 (which Mahinda Rajapaksa disclosed he did), the SLPP, conceived through opposing the 2015 coalition with Ranil’s UNP, supported Ranil Wickremesinghe instead, making him President. Thus, Ranil who was never elected President by the citizenry, was appointed to that post by Gotabaya Rajapaksa and endorsed by the SLPP—reloading Chandrika’s 2015 ‘hybrid’.

Ranil’s economic stabilisation/adjustment ‘shock therapy’ (2022-2024) further crunched the SLPP’s base after Gotabaya’s ‘fertiliser shock’ had shrunk it (2019-2022). SLPP voters shifted to the JVP-NPP.

When Namal Rajapaksa boldly broke away from the Ranil-led project and ran as SLPP candidate in 2024, elements of the SLPP and SLFP who had opposed the Yahapalanaya coalition, ironically stayed to support Ranil—mimicking Chandrika’s 2015 model.

title: Sri Lanka’s THC dispute: Regulating charges or regulating contracts? | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 5 November 2026 00:31
-     - 13

By Joint Apparel Association Forum

Sri Lanka’s recurring dispute over terminal handling charges (THC) has again set maritime service providers against the trading community, and each side claims to speak for the national interest. The Sri Lanka Association of NVOCC Agents (SLANA) told its 9th AGM that THC is treated as a separate land-based cost in international markets and asked the Government to expedite a committee on the issue (Daily FT, 14 September 2026). The National Chamber of Exporters (NCE) has urged that Gazette No. 2334/26 be retained, warning that a separate THC would reopen the fragmented system of “nearly 50” charges that existed before 2013 (Hiru News, 16 October 2026). The Ceylon Freight & Logistics Association (CEYFFA) has since said at a press conference that Sri Lanka “could be losing” more than $ 50 million a year in foreign exchange under the current framework (press report, 31 October 2026).

The task for Government is not to choose between shipping lines and cargo owners. It is to distinguish legitimate cost recovery from uncontracted charging, and commercial freedom from regulatory privilege.

1. Two legitimate arguments about different questions

The service providers’ case deserves a hearing. Shipping lines, NVOCCs, consolidators and feeder operators argue that terminal handling is a land-side cost, distinct from sea carriage, and that in many markets it is quoted and invoiced separately. They point to rising terminal costs, the expense of repositioning empty containers and the thin margins of NVOCC and LCL operators. CEYFFA adds a foreign-exchange argument: that dollar payments abroad and dollar billing by terminals strain local logistics firms and the country’s reserves.

The trading community’s case is equally legitimate. Exporters, importers and the Shippers’ Council do not dispute that port handling has a cost. They fear that intermediaries could invoice a charge to a cargo owner who never negotiated it, which is particularly harmful to SMEs with little bargaining power. The Sri Lanka Apparel Exporters’ Association made the same point when it warned in July 2025 against reintroducing THC not found in SLPA’s approved tariff.

The two arguments answer different questions. The first asks whether the cost can be recovered at all. The second asks from whom it may be recovered, and with what disclosure. A rise in operating cost shows that a cost exists. It does not show that the cost must be billed separately to a Sri Lankan importer or exporter. Separating the questions makes the dispute far easier to resolve.

2. What the law actually provides

The all-inclusive freight regime began with Gazette Extraordinary No. 1842/16 of 27 December 2013, effective 6 January 2014, and was developed through Gazette No. 2041/10 of 17 October 2017. The 2022 amendments under Gazette No. 2302/24 proved controversial, and Gazette No. 2321/62 rescinded the 2017 regulations and the 2022 amendment in March 2023. The Minister then issued Gazette Extraordinary No. 2334/26 on 31 May 2023, under section 10 of the Licensing of Shipping Agents, Freight Forwarders, Non-Vessel Operating Common Carriers and Container Operators Act, No. 10 of 1972. Its key provisions are these:

The Gazette does not abolish THC as an economic cost. It regulates how that cost is recovered and identifies the party contractually liable for it. A service provider remains free to negotiate the total freight price. The primary question is therefore whether a charge forms part of the agreed carriage contract, not whether its cost arose at sea or on land.

3. Two tests in sequence: The Incoterm, then the Gazette

Two layers of rules decide who pays. The first is the sale contract. Incoterms 2020, published by the International Chamber of Commerce, decide which of buyer or seller must arrange and pay for carriage: under FOB the buyer, under CIF the seller. They are contractual terms and do not govern the contract of carriage itself (Maersk summary of Incoterms 2020). The second layer is the contract of carriage. The party that contracts with the line or NVOCC pays the freight, and in Sri Lanka the Gazette requires that freight to be all-inclusive and recoverable only from that party.

THC is the terminal’s charge for physically handling the container: at origin, gate-in, yard move and loading onto the vessel; at destination, discharge, yard move and gate-out. In common practice it is “levied by the terminal, invoiced by the ocean carrier to the paying party” (GoFreight glossary). At Colombo, therefore, the handling element of the freight finishes with the terminal operator, paid by the carrier or its agent. SLPA announced in April 2022 that from 1 June 2022 it would collect navigation, stevedoring and terminal income from shipping lines in US dollars (Daily Mirror, 27 April 2022; the report cites no legal instrument).

One area needs care. Under FCA, commonly cited practice places origin handling on the seller as part of delivering the goods on board. For a Sri Lankan exporter selling FCA, the foreign buyer is the carriage contracting party, so on my reading of Regulations 3 and 7 a licensed provider may not invoice the exporter anything beyond the all-inclusive freight. The Gazette therefore governs whom a licensed provider may invoice. It does not stop buyer and seller from agreeing between themselves how the cost is shared. DGMS should confirm this reading in writing, because exporters and providers currently argue past each other on exactly this point.

4. What port-to-port freight actually covers

Port-to-port freight is more than the vessel. Basic ocean freight “covers the basic cost of transporting a container … from origin to destination”, derived from vessel cost, voyage distance and fixed costs, with fuel risk passed through a bunker adjustment factor and currency risk through a currency adjustment factor (Marine Insight). Behind every loaded box lies an empty one. Trade imbalances leave surplus empties in some places and shortages in others, and lines reposition them. Lines “typically absorb direct repositioning expenses as operational costs” and recover them “indirectly” through freight rates and surcharges (Docshipper).

The regulated scope is container yard to container yard. Inland haulage, including empty pick-up from the depot and return, depends on whether the carrier or the merchant arranges it (Hapag-Lloyd). It falls outside the carriage described in Regulation 11 unless the carrier is separately hired for it. Demurrage and detention beyond free time are also billed separately.

This explains why a label proves little. An illustrative quote of $ 500 ocean freight plus $ 150 in terminal charges is not inherently cheaper or dearer than an all-inclusive $650. The distinction matters only when a charge is added after the freight contract is concluded, or when the structure stops customers comparing quotations.

5. The feeder layer: SOC containers, FIFO and direct billing

Colombo is mainly a transhipment hub: about 80 per cent of its January to October 2025 volume was transhipment (Maritime Gateway). Regional feeders connect it to neighbouring ports and carry many NVOCC and shipper-owned containers (SOC). Freight terms in that trade vary. Under Free In/Free Out (FIFO) terms, loading and discharging handling charges are not included in the rate; under Liner In/Liner Out (LILO) they are (SeaRates glossary). The terms show there is no single universal way of quoting terminal handling.

Reports from 2022 show how this works in Colombo. For over 25 years, feeder operators paid port handling and terminal handling charges to the terminals on NVOCCs’ behalf and were reimbursed (Daily FT, 12 February 2022). Feeders then required NVOCC agents to obtain direct billing facilities with the three terminals, a requirement that arose from a dispute that reached ministerial level (Daily FT, 20 June 2022). The terminals reportedly wanted a separate US dollar bank guarantee for each principal at each terminal (Logistics.lk, 29 December 2022). NVOCC lines were reported to carry about 23 per cent of Sri Lanka’s containerised import and export volume in 2021, which is why the arrangement matters to trade.

The key point is the one Figure 3 makes: the same terminal cost can sit inside two different contracts. Between an NVOCC and a feeder, both are commercial parties and the freight term allocates the handling cost. Between an importer or exporter and a line or NVOCC, the Gazette requires one all-inclusive freight recoverable only from the party contractually bound. Treating the two as identical would be wrong in either direction.

The Gazette’s treatment of business-to-business feeder and SOC contracts needs clarification. Regulation 3 is broadly drafted, while Regulation 11 defines the regulated carriage by container yard and freight station movements. As I read it, there is no express carve-out for feeder-to-SOC FIFO contracts, so it would be premature to say that every separate port handling invoice between a feeder and an SOC operator is exempt. DGMS should state how the Gazette applies to those contracts without weakening protection against uncontracted charges on importers and exporters.

6. International practice cannot be adopted selectively

The industry is right that many lines list origin and destination THC as separate items. THC commonly appears as a separate line on quotes and invoices, and the Incoterm decides which party bears it. But the same sources note exceptions: under CFR and CIF, origin THC is included in the seller’s freight rate, and some door-to-door quotes bundle THC into a single price (GoFreight). There is therefore no universal international rule that THC must be separately invoiced, and no universal rule that it must be bundled. Colombo should be compared with competing ports on the total landed cost of moving a container, enforceable contractual terms and predictability of charges, not on the label attached to a fee.

7. The $ 50 million claim, tested

The CEYFFA figure is reported as “could be losing” more than $ 50 million a year. The report prints no calculation, period, container volumes or transaction data. Four points frame it. First, Figure 1 shows that the handling element of the freight ends with Sri Lankan terminal operators, which SLPA reportedly collects in dollars from shipping lines. What the carrier keeps is the ocean-freight element, earned abroad in every international shipment. Second, a complaint that terminals bill local firms in dollars concerns the currency of billing, a separate question that the all-inclusive freight rule does not address; Gazette 2334/26 names no terminal operators and its only currency provision is the rupee delivery order fee. Third, scale: Central Bank data reported by Maritime Gateway show about 1.10 million domestic TEU in January to October 2025, so $ 50 million spread across that volume is roughly $ 38 to $ 45 per TEU. That is a plausible order of magnitude, but a total divided by a volume is not a loss. Fourth, genuine leakage, when investigated, is quantified in accounts and transfers: Parliament was told in July 2026 of about $ 715 million remitted overseas through 105 shell companies and some 24,300 transfers (Daily FT). The claimants should publish their workings so regulators can reconcile them.

8. Competition is the missing regulatory test

The debate is usually framed as service providers wanting freedom against exporters wanting protection. A better question is whether a proposed arrangement promotes or restricts competition. Would separate THC help NVOCCs and feeders offer competitive services and let cargo owners negotiate a lower overall price? Or would it let intermediaries impose non-negotiated charges on captive consignees? The terminal side raises the same test. NVOCC agents say the 2022 terminal conditions, including a dollar guarantee per principal per terminal and insurance comparable to a vessel operator’s, are harder than conditions at regional ports (the NVOCC side’s account, not independently verified). Competition policy should prevent exploitation of contractual dependence without restricting legitimate price negotiation, on both the cargo side and the terminal side.

9. A balanced way forward

The Government should avoid blanket rescission of Gazette No. 2334/26 and instead:

1. Review before reform. Have DGMS review the charging arrangements with shipping agents, vessel operators, NVOCCs, consolidators, feeders, SLPA, the terminal operators, exporters and importers, using anonymised freight contracts, port invoices and comparable regional tariffs.

2. Publish a charge map. For each shipment type (import FCL, export FCL, LCL, feeder or SOC), set out in one page the contracting party, who invoices whom, in which currency and on what legal basis.

3. Clarify the feeder and SOC position under Regulations 3 and 11, preserving the prohibition on uncontracted charges to importers and exporters.

4. Settle the evidence on foreign exchange. Ask CEYFFA for its workings, and have the Central Bank, SLPA, Customs and DGMS reconcile them and publish the result.

5. Review terminal billing conditions for NVOCC and feeder cargo, including direct billing and guarantee requirements, from a competition standpoint.

6. Require any amendment to be precise. It should define its scope and safeguards, rest on the proper statutory authority and procedure, follow stakeholder consultation, and avoid creating a general right to recover charges from cargo owners merely because a provider can point to an underlying cost.

Conclusion: protect the contract, not the label

The THC dispute is not about whether port handling has a cost. It does. Nor is it only about whether the cost is collected locally or folded into ocean freight. The questions that matter are who contracted for the service, who is legally liable for the cost, whether the charge was transparently disclosed and whether its collection complies with the law. Sri Lanka needs a framework that protects traders against uncontracted charges while letting providers recover legitimate costs from parties that have lawfully agreed to bear them.

Colombo’s competitiveness will not be decided by whether a charge is called THC, PHC or all-inclusive ocean freight. It will be decided by the total cost of moving cargo, the predictability of commercial obligations and the integrity of the regulatory framework.
