title: Sri Lanka’s Rs. 2.1 trillion tax arrears: Collect, resolve or remove | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 5 November 2026 00:26
-     - 22

Sri Lanka has made significant progress in rebuilding government revenue following the economic crisis. Tax revenue increased from 7.3% of GDP in 2021 to 15.4% in 2025. Yet, behind this recovery lies an uncomfortable figure. Approximately Rs. 2.1 trillion is reported as taxes in default at the end of 2025, as per the findings published in IMF’s revenue administration diagnostic report. 

The obvious question is why the Government is not simply collecting this money? However, the Rs. 2.1 trillion should not be viewed as cash waiting to be collected. Approximately Rs. 1.6 trillion is under dispute, while IMF’s report also raises concerns over the composition and collectability of older arrears.

Before embarking on another collection drive, the Government therefore needs to establish what the Rs. 2.1 trillion actually represents.

Clean the arrears book first

The Inland Revenue Department should undertake a comprehensive internal analysis of the arrears stock, categorising liabilities by age, tax type, dispute status, recovery action already initiated, and likelihood of recovery.

Particular attention should be given to older debt. Section 161 of the Inland Revenue Act No. 24 of 2017 provides that: “Institution of action under this Chapter shall be commenced within five years of the date on which the taxpayer was in default.”

This does not necessarily mean that every tax debt disappears automatically after five years. The critical question is whether the required recovery action was commenced within that statutory period. Nevertheless, where five years have elapsed without such action, the legal recoverability of those amounts needs to be established.

If an amount is legally or practically unrecoverable, there is little merit in allowing it to remain indefinitely within the headline arrears figure. Such amounts should be moved into a separate doubtful or potentially unrecoverable basket and, following appropriate legal review and statutory processes, written off or extinguished where appropriate.

The objective is to arrive at a figure far more useful than Rs. 2.1 trillion: Sri Lanka’s net collectible tax arrears.

Resolve the Rs. 1.6 t dispute mountain

With around three-quarters of reported defaults under dispute, Sri Lanka has a dispute-resolution problem as much as a collection problem.

Cases should be segmented according to value, age, complexity, and prospects of recovery. Large, long-standing cases should receive priority, while relatively straightforward computational and interpretational disputes should be fast-tracked.

There may also be scope for a pragmatic, time-bound settlement program.

For both the Government and affected taxpayers, long-standing disputed arrears have effectively become a sunk cost. The Government has not received the cash, while taxpayers continue to carry unpaid or disputed liabilities. Pursuing the full amount for another five or ten years may produce less value than securing a substantial portion today.

The Government could therefore explore a carefully structured, one-off settlement window. Under this arrangement, taxpayers would receive a defined concession or discount, potentially on accumulated penalties and interest, in return for withdrawing disputes and settling the agreed liability within a short period. Any broader compromise of disputed principal tax would, of course, require a clear legal basis and safeguards.

Sri Lanka has experimented with tax amnesties and settlement measures in the past. The objective should not be another blanket amnesty that rewards non-compliance. Any new arrangement should come only after the arrears analysis, target identified legacy debts, include strict eligibility criteria, and operate for a limited period.

Done properly, this could produce a genuine win-win. Taxpayers could clear legacy liabilities and move forward, while the Government could convert ageing paper assessments into immediate cash. That cash could then support debt reduction, essential government expenditure, or productive economic activity rather than remaining trapped for years in disputes.

Lessons from elsewhere

International practice also demonstrates the value of distinguishing taxpayers who cannot pay from those who will not pay.

Australia permits payment arrangements for taxpayers experiencing financial difficulty, while retaining stronger recovery options where necessary. Compliance history and taxpayer engagement can influence the collection approach.

Canada illustrates the potential of digital debt management. Its tax administration enables taxpayers to arrange payments electronically. 

New Zealand similarly provides instalment arrangements for taxpayers unable to settle immediately and encourages early engagement where payment difficulties are anticipated.

The common principle is simple: intervene early, facilitate payment by viable taxpayers, and act decisively against deliberate defaulters.

Prevent the next Rs. 2 t

Cleaning up historical arrears addresses only part of the problem. Sri Lanka must simultaneously prevent another stock of uncollectible debt from accumulating.

The Rs. 2.1 trillion is not a static stock. It changes continuously as disputes are resolved and fresh assessments create new arrears. This makes the quality of assessments as important as collection. The central issue is whether new assessments represent genuinely recoverable tax or amounts generated through arbitrary or inadequately supported positions. To limit the future build-up of disputed and uncollectible debt, significant assessments should be subject to documented technical and legal review. High-value or high-risk cases should be cleared by a senior-level committee before being issued.

The strategy for addressing the Rs. 2.1 trillion should therefore be straightforward: collect, resolve, or remove.

Collect what is legally enforceable and economically recoverable. Resolve disputed liabilities quickly, including through carefully designed settlements where appropriate. And remove from the headline figure amounts that, following proper legal scrutiny, cannot realistically be recovered.

Sri Lanka has already asked compliant taxpayers to make a substantial contribution towards fiscal consolidation. Further gains should come from making the existing tax system work more effectively.

(The author is Partner, Head of Tax, Deloitte Sri Lanka and Maldives)

title: Proletarian, virtuous Bonapartism | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 5 November 2026 00:22
-     - 32

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake

“Unlimited power in the hands of limited people always leads to cruelty… The state was created to protect us from evil... but it generates others of its own, still more powerful, and this time one-directional” — Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, The Gulag Archipelago / The Red Wheel

  I voted for AKD. A profound sense of letdown compels this essay. In search of solace, I find myself turning to the old poets for refuge. It is a terrible thing when the dawn you so long-awaited deliver nothing but the same old midnight.

 I fervently hope that within the ranks of the 159 NPP parliamentarians, there remain at least a few who have read Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn’s The Gulag Archipelago and The Red Wheel. It is in that hope that I recall his timeless warnings in this essay.

 The titles of the two legislative masterpieces of the NPP Government, now awaiting debate and perhaps eventual passage, are eloquent.

  The first is called the Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill, and the second is the Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill.

 The term "Terrorism" famously defies definition. What, then, are organised crimes? And what are disorganised crimes? 

 Those wise words of US Supreme Court Justice Felix Frankfurter immediately come to mind:  “All our work, our whole life is a matter of semantics, because words are the tools with which we work, the material out of which laws are made, out of which the Constitution was written. Everything depends on our understanding of them."

 Both bills have already generated furious scrutiny. Distinguished scholars, including those rare individuals who possess the unique privilege of first-hand experience with "State Terror," have exposed the deep systemic dangers of these two drafts.

 I am no lawyer. I am no constitutional pundit either. But I do have a memory. I belong to the generation that witnessed our collective slide into the abyss of unreason following the passage of the original Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA). 

 I remember the legendary lawyer and Marxist politician Dr. Colvin R. de Silva describing his old classmate—the architect of the executive presidency and prophet of the PTA, J.R. Jayewardene—with the following immortal words: "The problem with Dickie is that often he runs faster than the winds that buffet him."

 As we watch President Anura Kumara Dissanayake navigate his ship of state, one is forced to ask the very same question: Is AKD running faster than the winds that buffet him? 

 In his frantic hurry to manage a fragile economy still in recovery mode, appease international lenders, and anchor his party's grip on the state, is he sprinting so fast into the arms of the old national security apparatus that he has outrun his own shadow?

 The parallel between J.R. (Dickie) Jayewardene’s executive velocity and AKD’s contemporary style appears obvious, instructive, and in this instance, quite chilling. 

 When JRJ assumed absolute power in 1977, he moved with a terrifying, calculated speed. He claimed that his radical restructuring of the state, the creation of the omnipotent Executive Presidency and the enactment of the draconian 1979 PTA—was a historical necessity to pave the way for economic liberalisation and to protect the nation from chaotic, destabilising forces. 

 JRJ ran faster than the gales of labor unrest and ethnic tension, outrunning democratic norms to build an institutional fortress for the ruling class.

 Today, AKD operates with a similarly breathless executive urgency. Faced with the howling winds of IMF restructuring, external debt traps, and the volatile undercurrents of public expectations, the National People’s Power (NPP) Government has seemingly abandoned the slow, cumbersome luxury of democratic consultation. 

 Like JRJ, AKD’s style is one of top-down efficiency; he behaves not as a subverter of the system, but as its ultimate authority—a kind of Supreme Arbiter! 

 The tragedy of the current moment is that while JRJ strived to build the national security state, AKD is sprinting to preserve it, proving that executive speed invariably leaves human rights far behind in the dust.

Reformer’s two scripts 

 What happens when the subordinate class finally scales the ramparts of the state and occupies the throne room? History offers two scripts.

 In the first, the victorious revolutionaries smash the old instruments of tyranny, declaring an unvarnished dawn of liberty. In the second—the more common, painfully predictable script—they look around the palace, realise how remarkably comfortable the executive chairs are, and decide that the old instruments of state control weren't actually not bad. They were just being operated on by the wrong people! 

With these two bills, the promised political renaissance is rapidly transforming from a progressive social-democratic daydream into a wonderfully Orwellian reality.

 During the 2024 election cycle, the NPP alliance, spearheaded by the modern Janatha Vimukthi Peramuna (JVP), marched to power on a platform of immaculate moral renewal.

  Their manifesto explicitly promised the total abolition of all "oppressive" laws, a blanket guarantee of civil rights, and the definitive burial of the infamous PTA.

Now, the Ministry of Justice has presented a parallel universe of legal wizardry. To the uninitiated, this looks like a flagrant betrayal. But that is because you do not understand the subtle, Orwellian dialectic of modern governance. 

 In this new dispensation, "Good Governance" is no longer measured by human rights charters or international legal certainty. "Good" is whatever the JVP Politburo decides is good on any given day!  

 If the old regime wiretapped you, it was fascism. If the new regime does it, it is a progressive prophylactic against social disorder.

The "State Terror" blueprint

 Nowhere is this legislative sorcery more sickening than in the actual provisions of the new Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill.

 For a nation that has spent nearly half a century suffocating under the old PTA, this new draft is an exercise in profound disillusionment.

 Instead of delivering the promised burial of counter-terrorism overreach, this bill replicates the fluid, all-encompassing definitions of "terrorism" that turn ordinary political expression into capital offenses.

 Under these provisions, the state reserves the right to classify acts of public protest, labor strikes, or civil disobedience as acts of terrorism if they can be framed as "disrupting essential services" or "coercing the Government".

 This is the foundational architecture of the garrison state. By leaving the definition of terror patently ambiguous, the bill systematically strips away the foundational due process guarantees that Sri Lankans have fought to preserve since the birth of our modern nation-state. 

 I have been told by knowledgeable people that this new law grants law enforcement sweeping powers of executive detention, allowing suspects to be held for prolonged periods completely severed from the vital check of immediate judicial oversight.

 Parallel to this is the jurisprudential innovation of the dress code and tattoo clause inside the Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill. 

 Under this innovation, courts can determine if you belong to an "organised criminal group" based on a highly subjective lifestyle checklist! Your style of dress, your vocabulary, your tattoos, or your physical and virtual associations.

 Sri Lankans will easily recall Naomi Coleman, the 37-year-old British mental health nurse who was arbitrarily arrested and deported simply for having a tattoo of the Buddha on her arm—an act the Supreme Court later ruled had absolutely no basis in law. 

If you sport a bizarre tattoo, use a pithy Sinhala expression that irritates a sensitive cop, or happen to accidentally join a Zoom meeting where someone holds a dissenting opinion, congratulations! You are now a potential asset of a transnational syndicate.

 This law effectively criminalises identity and association rather than concrete criminal conduct, turning every eccentric citizen into a potential threat to the state.

 It was the great Czech dissident Václav Havel who warned us about the unique horror of the post-totalitarian state, where the system demands total, unquestioning conformity to its arbitrary codes. 

 Havel observed that such a system forces the individual to "live within a lie," compelling ordinary citizens to act out rituals of obedience just to survive.

  A lawyer friend tells me that these two bills effectively "automate compliance". Our original PTA famously converted the land into a permanent garrison state; these new bills threaten to convert the remaining civilian spaces into an open-air prison where state wardens judge your loyalty by the ink on your skin and the words in your mouth.

 Then comes the absolute "gag" on the press. The bill makes it a criminal offense to publish the name or anything that could identify a victim of crime, while imposing heavy restrictions on media reporting of court proceedings without explicit judicial permission.

 The two bills constitute a masterpiece of authoritarian irony.

 A Government that swept to power on the backs of investigative journalism, alternative digital media, and public whistleblowing has now criminalised the very act of describing how the state prosecutes its citizens. The media is effectively told to sit quietly in the corner and print only the officially managed, sterilised truth.

Why the new vanguard must sprint

 To understand why the NPP feels absolutely forced to run at this breakneck, JRJ speed, one must look past the legislative text and peep into the vaults of the global finance markets.

 The unspoken crisis of the AKD presidency is the crushing, non-negotiable weight of the IMF’s Extended Fund Facility program that ends, and the new one that we are sure to end up with.

 When the NPP was in opposition, they vociferously criticised the devastating social costs of fiscal austerity, electricity tariff hikes, regressive taxation, and the fire sale of state assets. They promised a compassionate, people-first alternative. But the reality of state power is a brutal, sobering experience.

  Once in the driver's seat, AKD realised that the state machinery cannot survive without the next IMF tranche. The "Renaissance" must be funded, and the gatekeepers of global capital demand absolute compliance.

 This creates a terrifying calculus for a leftist Government. Adhering to the IMF structural adjustments means enforcing policies that inevitably compress the living standards of the working class, slash subsidies, and drive up the cost of survival. 

 The laws of political gravity dictate that such severe economic pain will, sooner or later, trigger massive social unrest, labor strikes, and public protests.

 And this is precisely why the Government is running so fast into the arms of repressive legislation. They are acutely aware that they are administering a bitter economic pill to the very population that elected them.

 To prevent the inevitable blowback from disrupting the IMF’s rigid fiscal targets, the state must preemptively fortify its defenses. 

 The vanguard must sprint because if the economic storm catches up to them before these security structures are locked in place, the entire edifice of their governance risks collapsing.

Dialectics of State preservation

There is a piercingly painful historical irony in seeing a movement born in anti-systemic rebellion morph into the supreme custodians of the exact same police stations, intelligence networks, and surveillance cells they once fought.

 Navigating painful economic restructuring compels the former outsiders to embrace the principle that the end justifies the means.

 To protect its own tenure and ensure economic stability, the state instinctively preserves and modernises its tools of executive detention, warrantless searches, and parallel criminal laws. 

The Minister of Justice is now tasked with writing laws that satisfy both the ideological expectations of a revolutionary vanguard and the demands of a deep-state security apparatus.  

He has crafted a legislative regime where the state retains all its old, terrifying, defensive teeth, painting them with a pristine coat of left-leaning "ethical management".

 The two bills have effectively synthesised the institutional paranoia of the old guard with the administrative discipline of the new left.

NPP’s renaissance, Orwell’s Animal Farm

 

The tragedy of this NPP "Renaissance" is that it validates George Orwell’s most basic insight from Animal Farm. 

 The pigs eventually stand on two legs, put on trousers, and the overworked horses outside can no longer tell the difference between the old masters and the new ones.

 Like Dr. Colvin R. de Silva’s "Dickie" Jayewardene before him, AKD is running faster than the winds of social and economic crises buffering on his presidency.  

But in his rush to outrun the storm, he is outrunning his own promises, leaving democratic safeguards far behind in the dust. 

 The parallel legal structures being built today are designed to bypass the ordinary safeguards of criminal law, allowing the Ministry of Public Security to bypass magistrates and detain citizens for up to a year on mere "reasonable suspicion".

 The next time you feel the urge to exercise your constitutional right to protest, or perhaps just write a critique of the regime, please remember you are now in a new Ethically Exemplary Orwellian Country. The State is always right. Saints are marching on.

title: Kusal Mendis, Udara rescue Sri Lanka with fifties | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 5 November 2026 04:20
-     - 13

ISLAMABAD: Skipper Kusal Mendis and opening batsman Lahiru Udara struck fifties apiece to help Sri Lanka declare at 223-7 on the opening day of their 3-day warm-up match against PCB Patron’s XI at Islamabad Cricket Club yesterday.

Sri Lanka, who elected to bat after winning the toss, recovered from a difficult start after losing three wickets for just 40. Mendis led a recovery with 66 providing the backbone of the innings. He struck 11 boundaries in his 72-ball knock, maintaining an aggressive approach despite the early setbacks.

Udara anchored the innings with 65 from 105 deliveries, including seven fours and three sixes. His contribution proved crucial after Pasindu Sooriyabandara fell for eight and Dinesh Chandimal departed without scoring, both to Saqib Khan.

Dhananjaya de Silva added 14 before becoming Mohammad Salman’s only victim, leaving Sri Lanka struggling at 40-3.

Udara subsequently combined with Mendis to rebuild the innings adding 90 for the fourth wicket before Ali Shabbir dismissed him for 65. Shabbir later removed Sonal Dinusha for ten to finish with two wickets.

Anjala Bandara hit an unbeaten 33 off 61 balls (5 fours) before Sri Lanka closed their innings.

Saqib was the standout bowler, returning figures of 2/28 from 12overs, while Mohammad Salman and Ali Shabbir also picked up two wickets apiece.

In the remaining 15 overs, Sri Lanka hit back through Dilshan Madushanka and Milan Rathnayake to capture two Patron’s XI wickets for 43 runs by the close.  

The match provides Sri Lanka with valuable preparation ahead of their upcoming two-Test series against Pakistan, scheduled to begin in Rawalpindi on 9 November, with the second Test in Lahore from 17 November.

Scores: 

Sri Lanka 223-7 decl. (Lahiru Udara 65, Kusal Mendis 66, Anjala Bandara 33*, Saqib Khan 2/28, Mohammad Salman 2/52, Ali Shabbir 2/28) against PCB Patron’s XI 43-2 at close.

Sri Lankan performance and lifestyle brand Carnage has extended its commitment to developing local sporting talent by supporting Team Sri Lanka’s contingent at the Youth Olympic Games Dakar 2026, reinforcing its growing role in the country’s sporting landscape.

The partnership forms part of Carnage’s broader collaboration with the National Olympic Committee of Sri Lanka (NOCSL), under which the brand was appointed Official Activewear Partner for major international sporting events, including the Youth Olympic Games Dakar 2026.

Team Sri Lanka is represented at the Games across four disciplines: athletics, swimming, badminton and taekwondo, with a contingent of athletes and officials carrying the country’s aspirations onto the international stage.

Carnage Founder Joel Tillekeratne said: “Supporting Sri Lankan athletes has always been close to the heart of Carnage. We know the talent our country possesses, and we believe it deserves the right backing to reach its full potential. As a Sri Lankan brand, we see it as our responsibility to contribute to that journey, not simply celebrate athletes when they make it to the international stage. Through our partnerships and the Carnage Athlete Foundation, we hope to make a real difference by giving athletes access to the support, resources and opportunities they need to develop their abilities and compete with confidence at the highest level.” 

For Carnage, supporting athletes at international competitions is about more than putting the brand behind a team. It is about being part of their journey, recognising the hard work that goes into reaching that level and ensuring athletes have the support and opportunities they need to compete, grow and succeed. Carnage believes that sporting talent deserves to be backed not just at moments of victory, but throughout the journey that makes those moments possible. 

The Dakar 2026 partnership builds on Carnage’s wider commitment to athlete development and sports in Sri Lanka in general. The Carnage Athlete Foundation is also a testament to this nationwide responsibility that the brand has taken on. Driven by the objective of, “inspiring the next generation of champion athletes”, the foundation has already extended its support to athletes across various sports and disciplines.

For Carnage, every athlete represents more than an individual pursuit of sporting excellence; they represent the potential of Sri Lankan sport on the global stage. Building that potential requires a collective commitment, with corporates playing an important role in strengthening the sporting ecosystem through investment, resources and opportunities. By standing behind athletes at every stage of their journey, businesses can help create a stronger foundation for Sri Lanka to develop world-class talent, compete internationally and earn its place among the best in the world.

From left: William Angliss Institute Australia CEO Grant Dreher, Tangerine Beach Hotels Chairperson Angeline Ondaatje and Jetwing Travels Chairperson and Managing Director Shiromal Cooray

Australian High Commissioner Matthew Duckworth

The Australian High Commission in Sri Lanka recently hosted the latest edition of its ConnectED Thought Leadership Series at the Australian High Commissioner’s Residence in Colombo, bringing together senior leaders from Sri Lanka’s tourism, hospitality, travel, events, education and related sectors.

The discussion, themed “Beyond Arrivals: Can Tourism and Hospitality Power Sri Lanka’s Next Growth Phase?”, focused on the role of tourism and hospitality beyond visitor arrival numbers, examining how the sector could contribute to Sri Lanka’s broader economic development.

The distinguished panel comprised Jetwing Travels Chairperson and Managing Director Shiromal Cooray; Tangerine Beach Hotels PLC Chairperson Angeline Ondaatje, and William Angliss Institute Australia CEO Grant Dreher. 

The discussion was moderated by William Angliss Institute Australia Director – International and Business Development Wayne Crosbie, who facilitated the conversation around the evolving needs of the tourism and hospitality industry and the importance of connecting education, skills development and workforce readiness with industry demand.

Adding a practical and experiential dimension to the evening, students from the Colombo Academy of Hospitality Management (CAHM) played an active role in delivering the cocktail reception for the distinguished guests.

Students from CAHM’s Commercial Cookery and Patisserie programs prepared a selection of special items specifically for the occasion, showcasing their culinary skills, creativity and attention to presentation. The items were developed and prepared by the students as part of their practical learning experience, allowing them to contribute directly to a high-profile professional event.

Students from the Hospitality Management program were responsible for guest service throughout the cocktail reception. They welcomed and assisted guests and delivered the service while demonstrating their skills in professional guest interaction, communication, food and beverage service, teamwork, presentation and hospitality etiquette.

The student participation reflects CAHM’s commitment to practical, industry-ready education, giving students opportunities to develop the technical and professional skills required to build successful careers in the hospitality and tourism industry.

By bringing together industry leaders and education stakeholders, the discussion examined how stronger collaboration between industry and education can help build the workforce required to support the sector’s next phase of development.

Prime Minister Dr. Harini Amarasuriya this week participated in the inaugural ceremony of the Bachelor of Hotel and Resort Management (Honours) Degree Program at the Sri Lanka Institute of Tourism and Hotel Management (SLITHM). 

The first batch of the degree Program comprises 65 students.

Addressing the occasion, the Prime Minister stated that the launch of the degree programme marks a historic milestone for SLITHM, reflecting the institution’s evolution from a centre of vocational excellence into a recognised contributor to higher education and professional development in Sri Lanka.

The Prime Minister emphasised that tourism is far more than an economic activity. It serves as a bridge between cultures, a platform for international engagement and a source of opportunity for thousands of Sri Lankan families. She noted that the tourism industry Sri Lanka aspires to build must create quality employment, support local enterprises, empower young people, expand opportunities for women and ensure that the benefits of economic growth reach communities across the country.

Highlighting the Government’s ambitious targets for the tourism sector by 2030, the Prime Minister stressed that achieving these aspirations would require more than infrastructure development and investment. A highly skilled workforce, strong institutions, innovative thinking and the commitment to excellence would be essential to achieving sustainable growth in the sector.

The Prime Minister also drew attention to the need to strengthen women’s participation in the tourism industry, emphasising the importance of creating opportunities for women to contribute to and benefit from the sector’s continued development.

The introduction of the Bachelor of Hotel and Resort Management (Honours) Degree Programme represents an important step towards strengthening professional education and developing the skilled human resources required to support the future growth of Sri Lanka’s tourism and hospitality industry.

The occasion was attended by the Foreign Affairs, Foreign Employment and Tourism Minister Vijitha Herath, Secretary and officials of the Ministry, Chairman and Members of the Board of Directors of SLITHM, Representatives of the University Grants Commission and the Higher Education Sector, the tourism and hospitality industry, academic staff, parents, and students who form the first intake of this degree program.
